newsitem.title: USA: FCC's Hundt sees unfinished business for 1997.
newsitem.headline: FCC's Hundt sees unfinished business for 1997.

text.p: Federal Communications Commission chairman Reed Hundt on Thursday sketched out a wideranging agenda for next year, emphasizing unfinished business from 1996 over new initiatives.
Congress passed the Telecommunications Act in February to overhaul the nation's phone regulations, but the FCC must craft a host of new rules to implement the law.

"Congress said it sought to establish a 'procompetitive, deregulatory' national policy framework for communications," Hundt said. "That is our mantra as we try to wake all markets from the slumber of monopoly and retail price regulation."

Work remains to be done on the Commission's plan to remove barriers to competition in the local phone market, craft a new standard for digital television and make available new communications spectra, Hundt said.

Hundt also said the commission would likely investigate liquor advertising on television, try to ensure schools get on the Internet, and improve political candidates' access to the airwaves, among other matters.
Earlier this month, the state of Alaska asked the FCC to outlaw broadcast advertising for hard liquor.
Hundt has said he favors such a ban if TV stations refuse to abide by a voluntary prohibition, but two other commissioners said they doubt the FCC has authority to act.
In his agenda, Hundt said the commission would respond to state and Congressional requests for an inquiry into liquor advertising on television.
Earlier this year, hard liquor companies ended their voluntary ban on liquor advertising and it is now up to television stations to voluntarily decide not to carry the advertisements.

Digital television remains on the agenda, Hundt said. On Tuesday, the commission adopted a standard for high-definition digital TV, but several important decisions lie ahead before consumers can tune in to the new format.

Digital transmission will allow as many as five programs to fit in the airspace previously occupied by a single TV channel. The FCC must decide if existing holders of TV licenses should get to control the subdivisions or if the air space should be reallocated in an auction or other process.
Hundt said the commission must enable "broadcasters to compete in new markets, which is necessary to preserve free TV in a digital age."
Convergence between cable television and telecommunications markets has not happened as quickly as some predicted, Hundt noted.
"Apparently it's no small job to create sufficient incentives for competition to dispense with the need for regulation of monopolies," he said.

Hundt also suggested that the FCC should explore ways of transfering responsibility for collection of the debt owed by auction winners away from the FCC to others. "The FCC is ill-suited to act as a banker," he said.
